messages.subject: negative LRT statistic value
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I am working on a multidimensional IRT analysis to find differential item functioning (DIF) in any of the items of a 17-item graded response likert scale.

To briefly summarize what we've been doing, we are basically locating DIF on the items by creating three nested models and comparing their goodness of fit to each other. We then use a likelihood ratio test based on their goodness of fit values (in this case, -2loglikelihood value) and chi-square and df values to see whether the differences between their -2loglikelihood values is statistically significant. When model 1 and model 2 are compared, a significant difference indicates DIF. If this happens, model 2 and model 3 are compared using LRT and a significance indicates nonuniform DIF (as opposed to uniform DIF). Model 1 is our most restricted model, model 2 is our least restricted model and model 3 is between models 1 and 2 in restrictiveness. The problem we are having is that we are getting negative values for likelihood ratio statistic, and we can not determine whether or not there is significant difference between the fit of the models because the LR test static is negative.

According to my understanding, likelihood ratio test statistics are not supposed to be negative. This may indicate that the sample size used is too small, among other explanations, but the LRT statistic should not be negative. We do not believe sample size is an issue since our analyses is based on a sample size of 600 something respondents.

Also according to my understand of LRT, the less restrictive model is theoretically supposed to fit the data better than a more constrained model. Therefore, the equation for the LRT statistic is: 2(loglikelihood(less restricted model)-loglikelihood(more restricted model)). However, the key difference here is that our output discloses -2loglikelihood values. (We are using IRTPro to obtain these -2LL values for each model). So we have been basically subtracting -2ll of model 2(least restrictive) from -2llmodel3(more restrictive). However, if working with just regular log likelihood values, you'd subtract model 3(more restrctive) from model 2(least restrictive). I am not sure how the -2ll in our data effect the calculation of this LRT statistic, and whether this is responsible for the negative LRT statistic value's we've found. On previous items, we did not find negative LRT statistic values when comparing these models (using -2ll for all models, model 1 minus model 2, and model 3 minus model 2).

If anyone has ANY idea at all, please throw it at me. Or any info regarding likelihood ratio testing. Can a chi-square value be negative (I don't think so)? So do we take the absoulte value of these negative numbers for our chi-square value?? please...HELP!

messages.subject_clean: parameter estimates for missing cells in multipleGroup
messages.body_plain:
Hi Leah,

This topic has come up a few times before in relation to 'vertical scaling' where groups are administered a set of different and common items in order to equate the groups based on common items (a missingness-by-design situation). I'll use this topic as a springboard into what's happening here and how these coefs should be interpreted (*spoiler*, the coefs are fine, and so are their standard errors).

Consider the following design:

------------------------------------
Group   Set-1  Set-2  Set-3
------------------------------------
G1           NA      1         0
G1           NA      1         1
G1           NA      0         1
------------------------------------
G2             1       0        NA
G2             0       1        NA
G2             1       0        NA
------------------------------------

In this design there are three individuals in each group, and NA's indicate that they did not answer the item. Here, only Set-2 is in common because Set-1 and 3 are either answered by G2 only (Set-1) or G1 only (Set-3). Hence, if you were to try and fit single group IRT models (e.g., with mirt() after using subset() on the respective data) then the function will complain saying something like 'an item contains completely missing data and is therefore useless'. multipleGroup() takes a slightly different look though, but is equivalent when thinking in terms of the likelihood functions.

As a prelude to be explained momentarily, it is imperative that all parameters in Set-1 and Set-3 be constrained to be equal across groups. This is because without this equality constraint the optimizer will essentially think that G1 contains enough information to estimate the associated group-partitioned parameters using only the subsetted data relevant to G1 and G2 (which they does not, as they only contains NAs in certain blocks). In fact, if you did not constrain the parameters across groups then the algorithms will almost surely spin out of control because the model will be badly identified.

So, when you constrain Set-1 and 3's parameters to be equal across groups you will get equal estimates for G1 and G2, however all the information about these parameters comes from the groups with the actual observed data. Hence, although there was no data for G1 in Set-1 all the information from the parameters came from the data in G2; so in essence the parameters completely borrowed the strength where data was available. Standard errors are only based on locations where data came from as well, and the coefs where groups contained no data are fine and essentially ghosted in from the available information due to the equality constraints.

I hope that makes sense, but please let me know if this still requires more clarification. Cheers.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Optimize function in parameter-by-parameter
messages.body_plain:
Unfortunately, this wouldn't help and would only serve to slow the estimation process down. The likelihood functions would still maximize to the same locations (if they didn't then something would be very wrong), so you don't gain anything by doing it piece-wise. Instability has more to do with the curvature of the observed-data log-likelihood than anything else, which really can only be fixed by including more empirical information (either by obtaining more samples, or including prior as a source of additional information).

Phil

messages.body_plain:
Dear Phil,

Currently I'm working on a project where we attempt to link two measures of a construct with the hopes that we can describe the longitudinal trajectory of the construct over a relatively long timespan. Unfortunately, the measures never overlapped, but at the waves before and after the switch, a couple of items that are conceptually close to the construct and external to the measures were administered.

What I have done so far is first, estimated a GRM to the two waves of data where the switch happens, including the two external common items that occur at both waves, and saved the parameter estimates.

Then, I've fed in all the data from the two measures of interest at all time points, and then estimated another GRM using my saved parameter estimates. The external items were not included in this GRM. I then saved the factor scores for further analysis.

My questions to you are as follows:

1) Is omitting the estimation of the external items in the scoring stage correct? I reasoned that because I am trying to get an estimate of theta, I only want to include the items that are directly relevant to the construct during this stage.

2) Is it reasonable to use the factor scores I saved in a latent growth model context? I have been reading the archives of this group (and they are very helpful), and I think that I read that this is ill-advised due to shrinkage. Do you have any suggestions? Although the first goal of the project is to describe the trajectory of the construct, we would also like to predict individual differences in it with covariates.

Thank you in advance for any advice,

Joanne

On Sun, Mar 13, 2016 at 6:37 PM, Joanne Chung <chung....@gmail.com> wrote:
> Dear Phil,
>
> Currently I'm working on a project where we attempt to link two measures of a construct with the hopes that we can describe the longitudinal trajectory of the construct over a relatively long timespan. Unfortunately, the measures never overlapped, but at the waves before and after the switch, a couple of items that are conceptually close to the construct and external to the measures were administered.

That's an interesting problem. Though if the items are conceptually close, is it reasonable to constrain their parameters to be equal then? That might help to scale the parameters a bit easier if that can be justified.

>
> What I have done so far is first, estimated a GRM to the two waves of data where the switch happens, including the two external common items that occur at both waves, and saved the parameter estimates.
>
> Then, I've fed in all the data from the two measures of interest at all time points, and then estimated another GRM using my saved parameter estimates. The external items were not included in this GRM. I then saved the factor scores for further analysis.
>
> My questions to you are as follows:
>
> 1) Is omitting the estimation of the external items in the scoring stage correct? I reasoned that because I am trying to get an estimate of theta, I only want to include the items that are directly relevant to the construct during this stage.

Yes this is fine.

>
> 2) Is it reasonable to use the factor scores I saved in a latent growth model context? I have been reading the archives of this group (and they are very helpful), and I think that I read that this is ill-advised due to shrinkage. Do you have any suggestions? Although the first goal of the project is to describe the trajectory of the construct, we would also like to predict individual differences in it with covariates.

It's okay to use factor scores for exploratory/suggestive reasons like this, so I wouldn't worry much. They just tend to break down when one is interested in unbiased inferences about parameters. That being said, you could always resort to plausible-value imputations to get around the problem for the most part (or at least lesson the shrinking effect), but I would do that at a later stage. Also, be sure to use MAP estimation if you have a number of latent traits (I couldn't quite tell from context). Cheers.

Phil

> Joanne

messages.subject_clean: mirt: standard error of b parameter
messages.body_plain:
As a follow-up to this message, if you really want the standard errors you can compute them via the delta method like so:

library(mirt)

name <- 'old2PL'
par <- c(a = .5, b = -2)
est <- c(TRUE, TRUE)
P.old2PL <- function(par,Theta, ncat){
    a <- par[1]
    b <- par[2]
    P1 <- 1 / (1 + exp(-1*a*(Theta - b)))
    cbind(1-P1, P1)
}
x <- createItem(name, par=par, est=est, P=P.old2PL)

dat <- expand.table(LSAT7)

mod <- mirt(dat, 1, 'old2PL', customItems=list(old2PL=x), SE=TRUE, SE.type = 'Richardson')
coef(mod, printSE=TRUE)[[5]]

## obtain via the delta method
mod2 <- mirt(dat, 1, SE=TRUE, SE.type = 'Louis')
coef(mod2, simplify=TRUE)$items[5,]
coef(mod2, simplify=TRUE, IRTpars=TRUE)$items[5,]

# extract required terms
parvec <- extract.mirt(mod2, 'parvec')
vcov <- vcov(mod2)
colnames(vcov)
pick <- 9:10
ad <- parvec[pick]
v <- vcov[pick, pick]

library(msm)
SEs <- deltamethod(list(~ x1, ~ -x2/x1), ad, v)
names(SEs) <- c('a', 'b')
SEs
coef(mod, printSE=TRUE)[[5]] #compare

Again, I have little interest in including delta method SEs for reasons that I don't particularly like the classical IRT forms, but you are welcome to obtain these manually if you are so interested. Cheers.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: multilevel multidimensional Rasch PCM model
messages.body_plain:
The likelihood is probably not well defined, so there's no strong unique solution but several equally good ones. I've played around with the PISA datasets before and I know they are pretty messy in terms of fitting models (and seem to be pretty riddled with multidimensionality).

As far as I can tell everything looks to be in order for PCMs when the data has well defined components:

set.seed(1)
N <- 5000
nitems <- 50
a <- matrix(rep(1,nitems),nitems,1)
d <- cbind(0, matrix(rnorm(nitems*3), nitems))
cluster = 200
random_intercept = rnorm(cluster,0,.5)
Theta = numeric()
for (i in 1:cluster)
    Theta <- c(Theta, rnorm(N/cluster,0,1) + random_intercept[i])

group = factor(rep(paste0('G',1:cluster), each = N/cluster))
covdata <- data.frame(group)
dat <- simdata(a,d,N, itemtype = rep('gpcm',nitems), Theta=matrix(Theta))
dat[sample(floor(length(dat)*.3), 1:length(dat))] <- NA

# null model
# mirtCluster() # to compute LL faster, if your RAM can manage it
mod1 <- mixedmirt(dat, covdata, 1, random = ~ 1|group, SE=FALSE, draws = 1)
summary(mod1)
coef(mod1, simplify=TRUE)

Phil

messages.body_plain:
Greetings,

        New user of mIRT here. From the workshop examples and manual I understand that it is possible to fit a one-factor and two-factor model to the data using

unidim <- mirt(scored.data, 1)
multidim <- mirt(scored.data, 2)

       Is there a limitation to the number of factors I can use? I am interested in trying to get a and b parameters (2PL) according to a six factor model; can the mirt package practically handle this command?
multidim <- mirt(scored.data, 6)

Thanks in advance.

Sincerely,
Colin Wee

University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign

messages.subject: Re: six-dimensional multidimensional IRT 2PL model - possible?
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Colin.

Why not? If your indicator variables can be explained by 6 latent variables theoretically, you can handle it. but, you have to change estimation method like this

mod1 <- mirt(scored.data, 6, method = 'QMCEM') or
mod2 <- mirt(scored.data, 6, method = 'MHRM')

Seongho
